mf.monthsToComplete.unit: months, start to completion, buildings with 20+ units (average)

mf.hardCostPerUnit.unit: USD per unit, construction value on permit, 5+ unit buildings

source.publisher: Terner Center for Housing Innovation, UC Berkeley
source.table: Development math presentation to CSAC, 4/22/2021 (prototype: land $65,488 of $573,569 per unit)

source.publisher: CBRE
source.table: Multifamily Underwriting Survey Q4 2024 (18 markets)

zoning.singleFamilyOnlyShare.unit: share of residential-only land where only a detached single-family home is allowed

source.publisher: The New York Times (Badger and Bui, June 18, 2019) using UrbanFootprint data
source.table: Cities Start to Question an American Ideal: A House With a Yard on Every Lot

spread.basis: city range in the NYT sample: New York 15%, Washington 36%, Los Angeles 75%, San Jose 94%

zoning.singleFamilyOnlyShare.notes: National Zoning Atlas reports about 81% of residentially zoned land in its covered jurisdictions is single-family-only (secondary citation, Vital City); multifamily allowed by right on about 12% (New America). The NYT URL was not loaded (paywall); the figures come from secondary summaries (UrbanFootprint, Planetizen).

zoning.minLotSqft.unit: square feet (land-area-weighted typical minimum lot, 1 acre)

source.publisher: National Zoning Atlas
source.table: Minimum Lot Sizes findings

spread.basis: median actual lot of new single-family detached homes 8,177 sq ft (NAHB/Census SOC) to Connecticut, where 76% of SF land requires >=80,000 sq ft

zoning.minLotSqft.notes: About 90% of single-family land has a minimum; over half requires 1 acre or more; about 3% allows lots under 10,000 sq ft. Large-lot share by state 26% (NC) to 89% (VT). Land-weighted figures are dominated by exurban land; in-town lots are typically far smaller. No national parcel-weighted median minimum found.

zoning.upzoningPermitEffect.unit: proportional increase in dwelling permits vs counterfactual after broad upzoning

source.publisher: Greenaway-McGrevy and Phillips, Journal of Urban Economics 136 (2023) 103555
source.table: The impact of upzoning on housing construction in Auckland (about 22,000 extra consents 2016-2021, per Auckland Council summary)

spread.basis: critique by Murray and Helm (curved trend: about 4,500 extra, roughly 10%) to the paper's estimate (about 50%)

zoning.upzoningPermitEffect.notes: Auckland upzoned about 3/4 of residential land. Minneapolis 2040 (triplexes): 2-4 unit permits +45% (avg 57/yr 2020-22 vs 2017-19, Bipartisan Policy Center), small in absolute terms; Minneapolis Fed (Oct 2026) counts only 47 projects using the change 2020-25. Effect of a lot-level duplex/triplex allowance alone is small; broad upzoning is larger.

supply.rentEffectPerBuilding.unit: proportional change in rents of nearby units (within about 250 m) after a large new market-rate building

source.publisher: Asquith, Mast and Reed, Review of Economics and Statistics 105(2): 359-375
source.table: Local Effects of Large New Apartment Buildings in Low-Income Areas

spread.basis: working-paper range 5-7%; published abstract about 6%

supply.rentEffectPerBuilding.notes: Buildings of 50+ units in low-income areas of 11 U.S. cities, measured 3-4 years after completion relative to units slightly farther away or near later-built sites; also raises in-migration from low-income areas.

source.publisher: Gabriel and Nothaft, Real Estate Economics 16(4): 419-429
source.table: Rental Housing Markets and the Natural Vacancy Rate (16 cities, 1981-85)

spread.basis: 4-10% across cities (exogenous spec), 7-12% (endogenous spec), as summarized in Hendershott, MacGregor and Tse (ERES 2001)

vacancy.naturalRate.notes: Housing Solutions Lab (NYU Furman) gives about 7-8% as a general rule. Gabriel and Nothaft (JUE 2001) later find a low, narrow range across metros.

vacancy.rentElasticity.unit: percentage-point change in real rent growth per percentage point of vacancy above the natural rate

source.publisher: not found in a primary source
source.table: model form: %dR = lambda (v* - v_t-1), Hendershott, MacGregor and Tse (Real Estate Economics 30(2), 2002)

spread.basis: none found

vacancy.rentElasticity.notes: I could not retrieve a U.S. apartment estimate of the adjustment factor lambda from a readable primary source (the papers that have it are paywalled; NMHC's 2024 note shows only a cross-market correlation). Make it a TUNABLE parameter fitted to Census HVS vacancy vs CPI rent; do not cite a number for it.

permits.perThousandResidents.unit: new housing units authorized per 1,000 residents per year

source.table: st2024a.txt (1,478,000 units) / NST-EST2024 (340.1 million)

inclusionary.setAsideShare.unit: minimum share of units in a new development required to be affordable

source.publisher: Lincoln Institute of Land Policy (Thaden and Wang, Working Paper WP17ET1)
source.table: Inclusionary Housing in the United States: Prevalence, Impact, and Practices, Table 13 / Figure 8

spread.basis: of 153 programs with a % minimum: 60 at 1-10%, 80 at 11-20%, 13 at 21%+; median falls in the 11-15% bin

inclusionary.setAsideShare.notes: 35% of programs vary the share by project; 90% allow on-site units; about 90% require affordability for 30+ years.

inclusionary.amiShare.unit: maximum household income as share of area median income

source.publisher: Lincoln Institute of Land Policy (Thaden and Wang 2017)
source.table: Income Served by On-site Affordable Units

spread.basis: rental programs with one maximum: 50-60% AMI (22), 61-80% (47, most common), 81-100% (9), 101-150% (16); 42% use multiple tiers; ownership up to 160%

inclusionary.rentShareOfIncome.unit: share of household income for affordable rent (incl. utilities)

source.publisher: U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development
source.table: PD&R Edge, 'Rental Burdens: Rethinking Affordability Measures' (Sept 2014): cost-burdened above 30% of income, severe above 50%; 30% set federally by the Brooke Amendment (1969, raised to 30% in 1981)

spread.basis: fixed policy rule; LIHTC applies 30% to the income limit for an imputed household size

inclusionary.rentShareOfIncome.notes: Rule, not an estimate. HUD defines 30-50% as cost-burdened and 50%+ as severely cost-burdened. URL found by search (the page is HUD PD&R Edge, Sept 2014); the exact path was not loaded, so check it before citing.

source.publisher: Schuetz, Meltzer and Been, Urban Studies 48(2): 297-329
source.table: Silver Bullet or Trojan Horse? The Effects of Inclusionary Zoning on Local Housing Markets in the United States

spread.basis: no single coefficient retrievable

inclusionary.productionEffect.notes: Findings are directional: no significant effect on price or production in the San Francisco area; in suburban Boston, IZ is associated with higher prices and lower production during regional price booms; affordable output modest and grows with years in force. Wang and Balachandran (Housing Studies 2023): 258 of 1,019 programs reported about 110,000 units in total. Make it a TUNABLE cost added to the builder's pro forma (set-aside share x rent gap) rather than a fixed production cut.

electric.costChangeDollars.unit: USD change in construction cost, all-electric vs mixed-fuel new single-family home (negative = cheaper)

source.publisher: New Buildings Institute (with NRDC)
source.table: Cost Study of the Building Decarbonization Code (single-family, NY cost data, climate zone 5A)

spread.basis: NBI $7,500-$8,200 cheaper; California 2019 low-rise residential cost-effectiveness study $6,171 cheaper (via City of Santa Rosa FAQ, secondary); E3 notes homes without air conditioning do not get the one-heat-pump-for-two-appliances saving (towards 0)

electric.costChangeDollars.notes: Savings come mostly from avoided gas service line and piping (NRDC cites about $6,000 average builder-paid gas connection in California). RMI 2022 (9 cities) finds all-electric cheaper to build in all 9 but its figures are only in charts. 'Electric-ready' mixed-fuel homes cost +$1,000-$1,800 (NBI).

source.publisher: Derived: NBI dollar savings / NAHB 2024 average construction cost

spread.basis: -$8,200/$428,215 to no saving (homes without AC)

electric.costChangePct.notes: No source states a percent directly; this is my arithmetic. Mark as ESTIMATED.

source.table: Land Values 2024 Summary (August 2024)

farmland.developmentShare.unit: share of all new development that occurred on agricultural land

source.publisher: American Farmland Trust
source.table: Farms Under Threat: The State of America's Farmland (2018), period 1992-2012

spread.basis: single national point estimate; no published range. (Of farmland lost, 59% went to urban expansion and 41% to low-density 1-20 acre residential.)

farmland.developmentShare.notes: 31 million acres lost 1992-2012, 11 million of it the best land. AFT 2022 projection (Farms Under Threat 2040): 18.4 million acres converted 2016-2040 on trend, 6.2 million to urban and 12.2 million to low-density residential; 24 million under faster sprawl.
